author: @empires.and.egos
caption:
That helmet is 500 years too late for the Odyssey.

The Odyssey is set around 1200 BC. The crested bronze helmet everyone
pictures is a Corinthian — roughly 700 BC. Five centuries later.

A real warrior at Troy wore a cap built from about thirty boars’ tusks,
sliced and sewn in rows onto leather, and carried a shield the size of a
door slung from his neck, because nobody had worked out how to strap one
to an arm yet. At Dendra they dug up the real thing: overlapping bronze
bands, 1400 BC, eighteen kilos.

And here’s the part nobody tells you. Homer did exactly the same thing —
he wrote four centuries after the war and dressed his heroes in the
armour of his own century. Except once. In Book 10 of the Iliad he
describes a boar’s tusk helmet, exactly right, an object already obsolete
for four hundred years before he was born.

Somebody remembered it. Out loud. For four centuries.

#greekmythology #trojanwar #bronzeage #mycenaean

author: @empires.and.egos
caption:
The Parthenon was painted. Red, blue and gold, like a carnival float.

We inherited Athens as white marble, and that is an accident. The
paint weathered off over two thousand years and Renaissance Europe
mistook the bare stone for the ideal — then built its own parliaments
and museums to match a mistake. The real thing was loud: painted
statues, gilded bronze, scarlet and blue picked out along every
cornice.

Then the temple became a church. Then a mosque. Then an ammunition
store, which is why it exploded in 1687.

Every empire dies wearing someone else's clothes.

#ancientgreece #parthenon #acropolis #historicalarchitecture

author: @empires.and.egos
caption:
Sparta’s soldier was the most feared in Greece. Then Rome turned the city into a tourist attraction.

For three centuries a Spartan hoplite was the answer to every question
about Greek warfare. Then the phalanx got longer pikes, then Rome
arrived, and Sparta became a client state that kept its old customs as
a performance for Roman tourists who came to watch boys be flogged at
the altar.

Every empire dies wearing someone else’s clothes.

#sparta #ancientgreece #spartan #historicalfashion

author: @empires.and.egos
caption:
Gladiators began as a funeral sacrifice. They ended as celebrity athletes with sponsors.

The first pair fought beside a grave in 264 BC — a private rite for one
dead nobleman, no arena, no crowd. Within two centuries the state had
taken it over. Fighters were classed by equipment like weight divisions,
trained in schools, and the best of them endorsed products and had
children named after them. Then Rome went Christian, the games were
banned, and the last of them walked out of an empty arena with nothing.

Every empire dies wearing someone else’s clothes.

#gladiator #ancientrome #romanempire #historicalfashion

author: @empires.and.egos
caption:
Rome’s soldier got heavier for 500 years. Then it got so heavy he couldn’t march in it.

The early republic sent men out in a bronze chest plate and a bare head.
By the empire it was banded iron, a curved shield, and a helmet with
cheek guards — the most recognisable soldier who ever lived. Then the
frontier stretched, the money ran out, and the armour came off again.
The last Roman soldiers looked almost exactly like the barbarians they
were paid to fight.

Every empire dies wearing someone else’s clothes.

#ancientrome #romanempire #romanarmy #historicalfashion

author: @empires.and.egos
caption:
Buried his father at 20. Dead at 32. Never lost a battle.

Eleven years, three thousand miles, and not one defeat — and forty
years after he died every descendant he had was murdered by men who
had served him. He planned every campaign and never planned the day
after.

#alexanderthegreat #ancientgreece #ancienthistory #macedonia

author: @empires.and.egos
caption:
An ordinary afternoon in Rome, 120 AD.

No emperor, no battle, no famous name. Just a street.

At its height the city held around a million people — more than any
European city would manage again for over a thousand years. The streets
were narrow, loud and filthy, the buildings went up four and five
storeys, and awnings were strung between them because the sun on the
stone was unbearable.

Almost everyone you can see here was poor, worked with their hands, and
left no record of any kind.

#ancientrome #rome #ancienthistory #romanempire

author: @empires.and.egos
caption:
Eight hundred years, and the last one looks like the enemy.

It starts in solid bronze — a chest plate hammered into the shape of muscles,
a helmet covering the whole face, a shield so heavy it was carried on the
shoulder. Then the metal comes off. Linen replaces bronze, the face opens up,
the kit gets cheaper because more men have to be able to afford it.

Under Alexander the spear becomes a pike twice the height of a man and the
shield shrinks to something strapped on the forearm.

Then look at the last one. Oval shield, short sword, javelin. By 150 BC the
Greek soldier is equipped almost exactly like the Romans who were about to
absorb him.

#ancientgreece #greekhistory #hoplite #ancienthistory

author: @empires.and.egos
caption:
Nobody voted to end the Republic. They voted, and it ended.

There was no coup. No foreign army at the gates. The Roman Republic
was dismantled by its own Senate, one legal vote at a time, and almost
every step was constitutional.

Dictator for six months, which was normal. Then dictator for ten years,
which was not. Then dictator for life, in February 44 BC. A gilded
chair. His face on the coinage. Each vote defensible on its own; the
sequence was fatal.

And then the strangest part. Rome kept the machinery. The Senate met
for another six hundred years. Consuls were still being appointed in
541 AD. Elections were held, offices were filled, the paperwork was
immaculate.

An institution can keep every one of its forms and still have stopped
being the thing it was.

#romanrepublic #juliuscaesar #romanhistory #ancientrome

author: @empires.and.egos
caption:
The Senate ran out of men rich enough to replace them.

After Cannae in 216 BC, Hannibal had his men strip the gold rings from
the Roman dead — the rings were worn only by equites and senators, so
each one came off a member of Rome's ruling class. Livy says they were
poured out on the floor of the Carthaginian senate by the bushel.

Rome lost around eighty senators in a single afternoon. To refill the
Senate they enrolled 177 new men, dropping the property qualification
and admitting the sons of freedmen. Then they armed eight thousand
slaves.

The Roman Republic did not survive Cannae by winning. It survived by
lowering the bar for who counted as Roman.

#ancientrome #romanempire #ancienthistory #romanhistory #history

author: @empires.and.egos
caption:
Rome's answer was to refuse peace talks entirely.

In 216 BC at the Battle of Cannae, Hannibal destroyed the largest
army the Roman Republic had ever assembled — roughly 80,000 men in a
single afternoon. More Romans died that day than Americans died in
the entire Vietnam War.

Then the Senate refused to negotiate, refused to ransom the
survivors, and banned the word "peace" in public.

Ancient Rome did not survive because it won. It survived because it
would not stop.

#ancientrome #romanempire #ancienthistory #romanhistory #history
